Question: Were all the particles created during the Big Bang entangled since they were formed together? If so, how could they evolve in time?
Answer: Entanglement as you describe can be simply recast as a universal wavefunction. We already know that wavefunctions evolve in time. A nonrelativistic example of this is the famous Schrödinger equation. Now what exactly do we expect with this universal entanglement? Entanglement manifests as a correlation between measurements. The entangled particles we tend to deal with in the lab are maximally entangled. That means they are maximally correlated. Now consider any two particles. Sure they can be considered to be a part of the universal wavefunction, but that doesn't mean they are maximally entangled. The degree of entanglement changes with every subsequent interaction. In general, just a single random interaction will alter the entangled state such that the correlation is no longer detectable. You could say that the entanglement has changed, but we don't know what that change is, so some information has been lost. Ultimately we can describe two types of entanglement: Useless entanglement because the correlations are too small to detect, so the information of entanglement is lost. This is regarded as decoherence. Useful entanglement. This is entanglement that is carefully prepared for use as a resource. In this case, unwanted interactions with the environment are essentially eliminated such that an effective isolated quantum system is created. This is what needs to be accomplished in the development of quantum computers.

Question: Assume that two photons (A and C) travel in opposite directions from point B. If an observer is sitting on A, then B will appear to be retreating at light speed. How fast will C appear to be retreating?
Answer: This will not give you a sensible answer simply because the photon is not a valid frame of reference. However, what you can do is consider massive particles travelling very close to the speed of light. In that case, the point B will appear to be retreating close to the speed of light and particle C will be retreating at a speed slightly closer to the speed of light. You see, the speed of light is an asymptotic limit to the relative speed between two massive objects. Once you drop to some finite speed below the speed of light, you can always go a little bit faster and still be below the asymptotic limit.

Question: What quantum principle is assumed in the manufacture of quantum computers - the Copenhagen interpretation or the many worlds interpretation?
Answer: Quantum computers are built based on the principles of quantum information science. This is agnostic to any interpretation, as interpretations are an attempt to describe an underlying reality. Quantum information science is based on measurement outcomes, which are empirical. Interpretations try to explain what measurements are. This is simply not needed to build a quantum computer. You just need the theory to predict measurement outcomes. Originally, David Deutch proposed that quantum computing demonstrated the many worlds interpretation, of which he is a prominent exponent. However, the development of quantum information theory is based on epistemology, rather the ontology, as information is an epistemic concept. So interpretations are not required to understand quantum computing.

Question: From quantum mechanics Einstein “hidden variables” vs Bell, what if it can be said quantum mechanics can “predict” which photons will be measured thereby restoring a “hidden variable theory” of sorts?
Answer: There is a hidden variables interpretation of quantum mechanics, which is the de Broglie-Bohm pilot wave theory. It is a non-local hidden variables theory, so is not ruled out by Bell's theorem. However, it has one major problem, and that is that all attempts at making a Lorentz invariant (relativistic formulation) have failed. If a non-local hidden variables theory cannot be made Lorentz invariant, then it is likely that this is not a viable approach.

Question: How many levels of quantum entanglement are there?
Answer: There are no levels of entanglement. There are however two broad categories of entanglement: environmental entanglement and local entanglement (these are just my heuristic categories). Environmental entanglement is useless because the entanglement is spread between too many systems. This means that the correlations associated with entanglement are too small to detect. This form of entanglement is ubiquitous and serves no real use (unless you are very clever- I know of one experiment where the entanglement with the environment was put to good use as a quantum memory using carbon-13 impurities in a diamond lattice). Local entanglement is that in which the interaction with the environment is minimised or eliminated. Such entanglement then can be used as a resource. In this regime, there are degrees of entanglement, from maximally entangled to non-entangled. This degree can be quantified using various measures, such as the tangle, entanglement entropy, concurrence, and others. These metrics are used when reporting experimental results, and are particularly important for characterising quantum logic gates. Entanglement can encompass multiple particles. However, the degree of entanglement reduces as the number of particles increases. This is referred to as monogamy of entanglement. The bottom line is that the degree of entanglement can be quantified. There is an upper limit, which is maximally entangled, and a lower limit, which is essentially non-entangled.
